mcqs.question: What organizational condition most strongly justifies adopting micro-frontends, according to the problem they're meant to solve?
options: A large number of teams share one app and need independent deploy/release cadences that a single shared build blocks
The app's bundle size has grown too large for a CDN to serve
The team wants to migrate from JavaScript to TypeScript incrementally
The app needs server-side rendering for SEO
mcqs.explanation: Micro-frontends exist to decouple teams' release cadences from a single shared build/deploy pipeline — the organizational driver is team count and cadence mismatch, not bundle size, language migration, or SEO, all of which have other, simpler solutions.

mcqs.question: A team wants each micro-frontend to deploy independently without requiring the shell app to rebuild, and without needing server-side infrastructure per fragment. Which composition approach fits?
options: Build-time composition, publishing each micro-frontend as an npm package the shell imports
Server-side composition stitching fragments into one HTML response
None of these — independent deploys always require a shell rebuild
Run-time composition via module federation, where the shell fetches and mounts each bundle in the browser at load time
mcqs.explanation: Run-time composition (module federation) is the only listed approach giving true deploy independence — a team ships by deploying their bundle, and the shell picks it up on next load — without needing the shell to rebuild or requiring per-fragment server infrastructure. Build-time still needs a shell rebuild, and server-side composition needs server infra per fragment.

mcqs.question: The shell app is pinned to React 18, but the checkout micro-frontend wants to adopt a React 19-only feature. Under module federation's shared-dependency model, what actually happens?
options: Module federation automatically upgrades the shell to React 19 for every user
The build fails permanently until every micro-frontend uses the same React version
Checkout either bundles its own React 19 copy (paying duplication) or the org coordinates the shell's upgrade together — sharing doesn't remove the need for version coordination
React versions are irrelevant to module federation since it only shares CSS
mcqs.explanation: Shared singletons only avoid duplication when versions are compatible; a genuine version mismatch forces a real choice between paying the duplication cost for that one dependency or coordinating an org-wide upgrade — exactly the release-train coupling the pattern was meant to avoid. Federation doesn't auto-upgrade the shell, doesn't hard-fail the build, and shares JS dependencies, not just CSS.

mcqs.question: Two independently-deployed micro-frontends need to share a selected filter value that should also be shareable via a link. Which cross-app communication pattern fits best?
options: Encoding the filter in the URL/query params, so any micro-frontend can read it without a direct communication channel
A raw DOM CustomEvent dispatched on window
A shared mutable global variable both micro-frontends write to
Neither micro-frontend should ever need to share state
mcqs.explanation: The URL is the most decoupled option and happens to be exactly right here, since the state is both navigable and shareable — no direct channel is needed and the link itself carries the state. A raw DOM event works for simple signals but isn't shareable via a link, and a shared mutable global reintroduces tight coupling the pattern tries to avoid.

mcqs.question: A team adopts micro-frontends expecting that a bad deploy from one team will automatically stay isolated from the rest of the app. What does the honest cost/benefit table say about this expectation?
options: It's correct — isolation is a guaranteed, automatic property of the architecture
It's only true if the team also switches to server-side composition
It's false by default — isolation (error boundaries per mount, no shared global mutable state) is engineering work that has to be actively built, not a free property of splitting deploys
It's false — micro-frontends make isolation strictly worse than a monolith in every case
mcqs.explanation: Every benefit column item in the comparison has a matching cost that must be actively engineered — isolation specifically requires per-mount error boundaries and avoiding shared globals; without that work, a crash can still take down the composed page. It isn't automatic, isn't tied specifically to server-side composition, and isn't strictly worse in every case — it's a trade that has to be earned.

mcqs.question: A company with two frontend teams and one mid-sized app adopts micro-frontends because the pattern is popular. What does this topic say about that decision?
options: It's the right call — any team count above one benefits from independent deploys
It's correct only if they also adopt a monorepo
It's correct because micro-frontends always reduce total infrastructure cost
It's likely the wrong call — two teams can usually coordinate a shared release train more cheaply than paying for contract testing, dependency negotiation, and duplicated infrastructure
mcqs.explanation: The pattern earns its cost at a specific inflection point — roughly double-digit teams or genuinely mismatched cadences — and below that, informal coordination is cheaper than the ongoing infrastructure micro-frontends require. It isn't universally beneficial at any team count, isn't fixed by pairing with a monorepo (a different, largely orthogonal decision), and doesn't reduce total infrastructure cost — it increases it.
